arguments.name: Vivid continuity and the reported Nelson–Barker exchange
arguments.position: Strongest conditional positive case with directly case-linked criticism and actual third-party reply
premises: Neal’s testimony describes continuous, vivid awareness and apparent rescue perception; the experiential attribution is supported, its external accuracy is not thereby established.
If independently fixed perceptions occurred without ordinary information access during measured absence of relevant brain function, this would challenge a strict dependence account.
The memoir’s named rescuers and individually conducted retrospective interviews are a stronger positive lead than unnamed retelling, but they remain narrated method and testimony.
bridge_principles: Move from seeming to external perception only with independent event/information controls.
Move from elapsed rescue time to neural incapacity only with relevant physiological evidence.
arguments.conclusion: The positive case is worth exact documentation; the present packet supports attributed experience and a conditional argument, not survival.
arguments.strongest_objection: Nelson’s reported distinction separates vivid memory from interpretation; REM intrusion/hypoxia is a possible alternative. Unknown timing and later information exposure undermine a uniquely survival-based inference.
arguments.strongest_reply: Barker’s actual reply grants that brain states might be present yet argues correlates need not determine interpretation; first-person quality deserves consideration. This blocks an automatic dismissal but supplies no missing Neal measurements.
unresolved_issues: Neural/circulatory timing; information exposure; independently preserved first witness report.
No raw2013panel recording; actual reply is Barker’s, not Neal’s and not an empirical adjudication.
General Mays rejoinder remains inherited broader debate, not direct corroboration.
Named rescuer detail does not itself supply an independent first record; later hospital/PCU conversations are distinct from the river event.

arguments.name: Rescue interval and clinical inference
premises: The memoir gives a reported eleven-to-fourteen-minute interval after missing-person headcounts; the SRT gives fifteen minutes after rescuers inferred the location; CNN calls the total an estimate.
Available medical wording is narrator/reporter assertion; submersion, oxygen availability, circulation and neural state are different variables.
bridge_principles: Elapsed rescue time alone cannot substitute for physiological measurement.
A source saying it reviewed records does not make those originals inspected here.
arguments.conclusion: Retain testimony and reported recovery; withhold a synchronized medical reconstruction and specific process exclusion.
arguments.strongest_objection: Neal identifies rescue-trained Long family members and reports listening to each individually, while the book gives a watch range and substantial injury detail. Those specific reports deserve assessment and could guide public corroboration.
arguments.strongest_reply: The actual versions differ in timing and start events; no original timekeeper account resolves them. Specific testimony is not a synchronized physiological record. Later reported saturation or no-injury assertions do not date river awareness to absent neural function.
unresolved_issues: Conflicting exact accident dates and age; no original timekeeper.
No temperature/chart/EEG or medication record; no private requests authorized.
ICU and river differ; later complaints/testing are not a single synchronous outcome.
Memoir eleven-to-fourteen versus SRT fifteen minutes; memoir hospital values remain unverified and distinct from river physiology.

arguments.name: Prediction, fulfillment and prior documentation
premises: Neal retrospectively reports knowing her oldest son would die.
Dated newspaper reporting supports a2009death report, while inspected prediction disclosure is later.
No inspected independent record fixes prediction wording, deadline, cause and scoring set beforehand.

The memoir narrates early disclosure and a pre-notification manuscript save, but also uses inconsistent first/final draft labels; its distinct child-not-eighteen story is not literally fulfilled within the same account.
bridge_principles: Independent fulfillment does not date or validate a prediction.
Absence of a retrieved advance record is an access limit, not proof no such record exists.
Repeated assertions and river/ICU conversations cannot be summed as independent successes.
arguments.conclusion: Retain attributed prediction and documented reporting chronology; withhold verified foreknowledge and odds.
arguments.strongest_objection: The strongest countercase to a successful-prediction reading combines postevent access to all detailed accounts, missing predated wording/scoring, internally different manuscript labels, and the separate age-specific child prediction followed by a changed-plan interpretation. Unknown counts prevent a rate calculation in either direction.
arguments.strongest_reply: Neal reports early confidants and a manuscript before learning of the death, and interprets some foreknowledge as involving changeable plans. These are meaningful positive claims to preserve, but presently only retrospective; a flexible-plan reply needs a prior scoring rule to establish predictive accuracy.
unresolved_issues: Original 2011 edition and any independent prefulfillment manuscript/confidant record remain uninspected.
2012-version spring first draft/final June21 versus Q&A first complete draft labels are unresolved.
Child prediction is distinct from Neal’s directive and is not an externally verified failure count. All numeric prediction values remain null.
